todayInHistory.title: Sam Laud
todayInHistory.text: Sam Laud Bay Shipbuilding Corp. of Sturgeon Bay, WI, laid the keel for their hull # 712 on Jan. 4, 1974 to be built as a smaller-sized Great Lakes self-unloading bulk cargo carrier. The new vessel was launched on Nov. 19, 1974 for Buffalo's American Steamship Co. (ASC), a subsidiary of GATX Corp., Chicago, IL. Completed in 1975, the self-unloader was christened Sam Laud by Mrs. Edna Laud on behalf of her husband at a christening ceremony held April 15, 1975. Mr. Laud was the former president (1945) and chairman of the board (1956) of GATX Corp., having started with the company in 1916 as shop painter and riveter. Mr. Laud died August 1, 1963. GATX Corp. had acquired ASC in July of 1973. Mrs. Laud was accompanied by Mr. Frederick G. Jaicks, chairman and CEO of Inland Steel Co., Chicago, IL, who gave the address at the christening ceremonies. One of a new generation of self-unloaders for the ASC fleet, the Sam Laud was built at an approximate cost of $13.3 million and was the fourth of 10 self-unloaders launched for the fleet under Chapter XI of the Merchant Marine Act of 1970. Under this act, the U.S. government-guaranteed financing and tax deferred benefits for fleet modernizing. The other ASC self-unloaders built under this program were the Roger M. Kyes (now Adam E. Cornelius, 1973), Charles E. Wilson (now John J. Boland, 1973), H. Lee White (1974), St. Clair (1976), Belle River (now Walter J. marineWeather.synopsis: 30.5 inch high pressure will stretch from New England to Texas while a 29.1 inch low moves into Hudson Bay today, putting Lake Superior around 30.0 inches between these features. High pressure gradually strengthens to 30.6 inches over the Canadian Maritimes through Monday as 30.4 inch ridge extends southwest to the Tennessee Valley. Meanwhile, 30.2 inch high pressure builds over the Northern Plains Sunday night and tracks east across Ontario at 30.4 inches on Monday, strengthening to 30.5 inches over Quebec by Tuesday. As this occurs, ridging over Lake Superior will strengthen from 30.1 inches tonight to 30.4 inches Monday night into Tuesday. Ridging then weakens to 30.1 inches over the lake on Wednesday as a 29.7 inch trough crosses Hudson Bay.
marineWeather.warning:

AFTERNOON

marineWeather.synopsis: Strong high pressure around 30.6 inches will slowly move east through the northeast US today. Strong low pressure around 29.2 inches will move eastward into Hudson Bay today while deepening to around 29.0 inches. This will bring southwest gales to far northern portions of Lake Michigan now into tonight. A Gale Warning is in effect during this period for the northern third of Lake Michigan but we have expanded the Gale Warning southward a bit to include the entire north half as wind appear likely to be a bit more expansive than originally expected. Building waves are also expected during this period. High pressure around 30.5 inches will then develop east-northeast of the region this week, bringing dry conditions and light to modest winds.
marineWeather.warning: GALE WARNING IN EFFECT THROUGH LATE TONIGHT

marineWeather.synopsis: A ridge of high pressure settles across the Ohio Valley today. This produces gusty westerly winds through the day as deep low pressure tracks across northern Ontario. The high pressure then builds northward and stalls over the Great Lakes through the middle of the week.
High pressure will persist through this week, weakening slightly from 30.50 inches to 30.30 inches.

A ridge averaging 30.2 inches affects the lake through this Thursday. One embedded high pressure center should wobble northeastward from the southern Great Plains to near Newfoundland through tonight. Another embedded and reinforcing high pressure center should move from near the border of the north-central United States and Canada to near the Canadian Maritimes this Monday through Wednesday. A third embedded and reinforcing high pressure center should move eastward from the Canadian Prairies to near the border of Ontario and Quebec this Wednesday through Thursday.
